title: Translation Assessment: Proust's Madeleine Passage in Urdu
subtitle: An editorial assessment report for interested readers and publishers. Segment-level deviation analysis on an error typology adapted from Multidimensional Quality Metrics, the translation industry's standard framework, for an expressive (literary) text, with a descriptive translation-studies profile of the translator.
sampleLocation: the madeleine episode in the Overture of Swann's Way; chapter manuscript pp. 40–42
author: Marcel Proust

source.label: Moncrieff
source.text: Many years had elapsed during which nothing of Combray, save what was comprised in the theatre and the drama of my going to bed there, had any existence for me, when one day in winter, as I came home, my mother, seeing that I was cold, offered me some tea, a thing I did not ordinarily take. I declined at first, and then, for no particular reason, changed my mind. She sent out for one of those short, plump little cakes called 'petites madeleines,' which look as though they had been moulded in the fluted scallop of a pilgrim's shell. And soon, mechanically, weary after a dull day with the prospect of a depressing morrow, I raised to my lips a spoonful of the tea in which I had soaked a morsel of the cake. No sooner had the warm liquid, and the crumbs with it, touched my palate than a shudder ran through my whole body, and I stopped, intent upon the extraordinary changes that were taking place. An exquisite pleasure had invaded my senses, but individual, detached, with no suggestion of its origin. And at once the vicissitudes of life had become indifferent to me, its disasters innocuous, its brevity illusory — this new sensation having had on me the effect which love has of filling me with a precious essence; or rather this essence was not in me, it was myself. I had ceased now to feel mediocre, accidental, mortal. Whence could it have come to me, this all-powerful joy? I was conscious that it was connected with the taste of tea and cake, but that it infinitely transcended those savours, could not, indeed, be of the same nature as theirs. Whence did it come? What did it signify? How could I seize upon and define it?

submission.label: Unnamed translator
submission.text: کئی برس گزر چکے تھے، جن میں کومبرے کا کچھ بھی میرے لیے موجود نہ رہا تھا، سوائے اس کے جو وہاں میرے بستر پر جانے کے تھیٹر اور ڈرامے میں شامل تھا؛ کہ ایک دن سردیوں میں، جب میں گھر لوٹا، میری ماں نے مجھے سرد دیکھ کر چائے پیش کی، جو میں عموماً نہیں پیتا تھا۔ پہلے میں نے انکار کیا، پھر کسی خاص سبب کے بغیر اپنا ارادہ بدل لیا۔ انہوں نے ان چھوٹی، موٹی، گول سی کیکوں میں سے ایک منگوائی جنہیں “پتیت مادَلین” کہتے ہیں، اور جو یوں لگتی ہیں جیسے کسی زائر کے صدف کے دندانے دار سانچے میں ڈھالی گئی ہوں۔ جلد ہی، ایک بے رنگ دن کی تھکن اور اداس کل کے امکان کے ساتھ، میں نے تقریباً مشینی انداز میں چائے کا ایک چمچ اپنے ہونٹوں تک اٹھایا، جس میں میں نے کیک کا ایک ٹکڑا بھگو رکھا تھا۔ جونہی وہ گرم مائع، اور اس کے ساتھ کیک کے ریزے، میرے تالو سے لگے، میرے پورے بدن میں ایک لرزش دوڑ گئی؛ اور میں ٹھہر گیا، ان غیر معمولی تبدیلیوں پر متوجہ جو میرے اندر واقع ہو رہی تھیں۔ ایک نفیس لذت نے میرے حواس پر قبضہ کر لیا تھا؛ مگر وہ منفرد تھی، الگ تھلگ، اپنی اصل کا کوئی اشارہ دیے بغیر۔ اور فوراً زندگی کے اتار چڑھاؤ میرے لیے بے معنی ہو گئے، اس کی آفتیں بے ضرر، اس کی مختصری فریب؛ اس نئے احساس نے مجھ پر وہی اثر کیا جو محبت کرتی ہے، یعنی مجھے ایک قیمتی جوہر سے بھر دینا؛ یا یوں کہیے، یہ جوہر مجھ میں نہیں تھا، وہ خود میں تھا۔ اب میں نے اپنے آپ کو معمولی، اتفاقی، فانی محسوس کرنا چھوڑ دیا تھا۔ یہ قادرِ مطلق مسرت میرے پاس کہاں سے آئی تھی؟ مجھے شعور تھا کہ اس کا تعلق چائے اور کیک کے ذائقے سے ہے، لیکن وہ ان ذائقوں سے لامحدود طور پر بڑھ کر تھی؛ بلکہ ان ہی کی نوعیت کی ہو ہی نہیں سکتی تھی۔ یہ کہاں سے آئی؟ اس کا مطلب کیا تھا؟ میں اسے کیسے پکڑوں، کیسے متعین کروں؟

deviations.note: منفرد means distinctive or unique; the source's "individual" means single, standing on its own.

suggestion.ai: ایک نفیس لذت میرے حواس پر چھا گئی تھی، مگر اکیلی، الگ تھلگ، اپنی اصل کا کوئی اشارہ دیے بغیر۔

segments.source: And at once the vicissitudes of life had become indifferent to me, its disasters innocuous, its brevity illusory —

deviations.note: مختصری is not an Urdu word, so "its brevity" is lost from the triad.
بے معنی ("meaningless") is stronger than "indifferent to me", which describes the narrator's detachment, not life's lack of meaning.

بھر دینا is left as a dangling infinitive.

segments.source: Whence could it have come to me, this all-powerful joy?
segments.submission: یہ قادرِ مطلق مسرت میرے پاس کہاں سے آئی تھی؟

deviations.note: قادرِ مطلق is a usual title of God, giving the joy a religious weight "all-powerful" doesn't carry.
آئی تھی ("had come") drops the wondering "could it have".

profileSummary: The minor deviations are small and scattered. Most are single-word additions (A2: #1, #4, #5, #6), with small slips in Urdu grammar and clarity (B1, B3: #2, #4, #9) and in tense or modality (A4: #11, #15). The critical and the major deviation both fall at the passage's philosophical climax: a mistranslated pronoun phrase in #9 (A1) and a non-word in #8 (B2). Together they change what the key sentence says. There are no omissions (A3) or changes to the logic between clauses (A6), and {clean} of {segments} segments ({cleanPct}%) carry no deviation.
tendencies:
The submission reproduces the shape of the English sentences in Urdu (C4 interference). This is a habit of the whole sample, not of single words.

- **Sentence architecture.** It keeps the source's sentence boundaries and clause order, and attaches descriptions after the noun with جو as English does (1.5 per 100 words in the passage, 1.0 across the chapter). Proust's long sentences arrive as chains of clauses rather than as a single movement.
- **Calques and punctuation.** The English article and possessive are carried over as ایک (2.3 per 100 words in the passage, 1.0 across the chapter) and میرے (2.3 and 0.7), and semicolons follow the source (1.7 and 1.3). Read across a book, the English stays visible beneath the Urdu.
- **Register (C1).** It settles into formal Persianate vocabulary (متوجہ، واقع ہو رہی تھیں، قادرِ مطلق، گرم مائع), slightly above the source's plain, intimate narration.
- **Logical links.** Links between clauses are kept as the source states them, neither added nor dropped. This is the main reason the deviation count stays low.

Counts are from the 343-word passage and from the full chapter manuscript (about 23,500 words, with sentences averaging 42 words).
translatorProfile: **Competent but mechanical.** The submission works by formal equivalence throughout. Interference from the source shows as the default setting rather than a choice, and a mild ennoblement appears in its Persianate vocabulary. Its apparent purpose is a faithful crib of Moncrieff for readers who want the content intact, **not a literary Urdu Proust**. Its deviations look accidental rather than chosen and the worst one comes exactly where understanding, not diligence, is tested (#9). The pattern is consistent with lightly edited machine output.
findingsLead: These belong to the translation as a whole, not to single segments.

The penalty is concentrated: the critical deviation in #9 inverts the turn the paragraph builds to, and #8 loses "its brevity" to a non-word, while the {minor} minor deviations are scattered. Accuracy elsewhere ({clean} segments with no deviation) argues against a weak grasp of English, so the same translator could undertake the retranslation. The errors at the central sentence (#8, #9) keep that a close call. If machine drafting were confirmed, a different translator would be advised.
